s: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Federal Court (inaugurated on 1 October 1937)?
x: Sir Maurice Gwyer was the first Chief Justice of the Federal Court, which the Supreme Court replaced in 1950.

s: Which of the following provinces was NOT among the six provinces provided with bicameral legislatures under the Government of India Act, 1935?
x: Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and the United Provinces had bicameral legislatures. Punjab was not included in this group.

s: How many sections did the Government of India Act, 1935 contain?
x: The Government of India Act, 1935 had 321 sections, 14 parts and 10 schedules.

s: Which provision of the Government of India Act, 1935 was never implemented?
o: Federal and Provincial Public Service Commissions
x: Dyarchy at the Centre was never implemented because the Federation did not come into operation; provincial autonomy and the Federal Court were implemented.

s: From when did responsible governments in the provinces under the Government of India Act, 1935 come into force?
x: The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy, and ministries answerable to the legislatures took office from April 1937.

s: On which discussions was the Government of India Act, 1935 primarily based?
o: First Round Table Conference and the Simon Commission Report
Third Round Table Conference and the White Paper
Second Round Table Conference and the Nehru Report
Cabinet Mission and the Cripps Proposals
x: The Government of India Act, 1935 was based on the Third Round Table Conference and the White Paper.

s: Why did the All India Federation proposed by the Government of India Act, 1935 never come into existence?
o: The Federal Court declared it invalid
x: Accession of the princely states was optional, and since no princely state joined, the Federation never came into operation.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, what was the position of Defence and Foreign Affairs?
o: Federal subjects under the federal legislature
x: Defence and foreign affairs were reserved subjects under the Governor-General, not the federal legislature.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the central legislature was to consist of the Federal Assembly and which other House?
x: The 1935 Act's bicameral Centre was the Federal Assembly plus the Council of States; communal representation was also extended to depressed classes, women and labour.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, from which province was Sindh separated?
x: The 1935 Act separated Burma from India, Sindh from Bombay and Orissa from Bihar.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched in relation to the Government of India Act, 1935?
o: Council of India — Continued without alteration
x: The Council of India created under the Government of India Act, 1858 was abolished, and the Secretary of State was provided with advisers.

s: Which one of the following provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935 was borrowed into the Constitution of India in substantially corresponding form?
o: The separate colonial status of Burma
The compulsory accession of princely states
x: The federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details were among the features carried into the Constitution. Compulsory accession and non-operational dyarchy were not borrowed as constitutional arrangements.

s: Under which Act was the Reserve Bank of India formed on 1 April 1935?
x: The 1935 Act provided for the RBI, but the bank was formed on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934.

s: Article 175 of the Constitution (Governor's address) corresponds to which Section of the Government of India Act, 1935?
x: Section 63 of the 1935 Act dealt with the Governor's address, now Article 175; Section 42 is the ordinance model for Article 123.

s: Which Section of the Government of India Act, 1935 is the model for the President's ordinance power under Article 123?
x: Section 42 of the 1935 Act is the model for Article 123; the Act's All-India Federation and Central Dyarchy were never implemented.

s: In which year was the Federal Court set up under the 1935 Act replaced by the Supreme Court?
x: The Federal Court, inaugurated in 1937, was replaced by the Supreme Court in 1950.

s: To about what share of the population did the Government of India Act, 1935 extend the franchise?
x: The franchise rose from about 3% to about 14% of the population (about 3.5 crore voters).

s: To which groups did the Government of India Act, 1935 extend communal representation?
o: Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans
x: The 1935 Act extended communal representation to depressed classes, women and labour; the 1919 Act had covered Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Government of India Act, 1935?
o: Defence and Foreign Affairs were placed under the federal legislature.
It provided bicameral legislatures in six provinces.
It vested residuary powers in the Governor-General.
x: Defence and Foreign Affairs were reserved subjects under the Governor-General, not the federal legislature.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, what happened to the Council of India?
o: Merged with the Board of Control
x: The 1935 Act abolished the Council of India and gave the Secretary of State advisers instead.

s: Which Act separated Burma from British India?
x: The Government of India Act, 1935 separated Burma from India and also created Sindh and Orissa as provinces.

s: In which year was the Federal Court, set up under the Government of India Act, 1935, inaugurated?
x: The Federal Court at Delhi was inaugurated on 1 October 1937 with Sir Maurice Gwyer as first Chief Justice.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, from which province was Orissa separated?
x: The 1935 Act separated Burma from India, Sindh from Bombay and Orissa from Bihar.

s:
Match the following (Government of India Act, 1935):
List-I (Territory)
A. Burma
B. Sindh
C. Orissa
List-II (Separated from)
1. Bombay
2. Bihar
3. British India
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: The 1935 Act separated Burma from British India, Sindh from Bombay and Orissa from Bihar.

s: Into which three lists did the Government of India Act, 1935 divide powers?
x: The 1935 Act made Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists, with residuary powers with the Governor-General.

s: Which of the following Public Service Commissions was NOT provided under the Government of India Act, 1935?
x: The 1935 Act provided for a Federal PSC, Provincial PSCs and Joint PSCs for two or more provinces.

s: Which Act ended provincial dyarchy, introduced in 1919?
x: The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy and brought provincial autonomy; dyarchy at the Centre never took effect.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: First Supreme Court at Fort William – 1774
First Law Member of the Governor-General's Council – Sir Elijah Impey
First Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Fort William – Sir Elijah Impey
Section 87 of the Charter Act, 1833 – opened Company service to Indians without discrimination
x: Macaulay, not Sir Elijah Impey, was the first Law Member; Impey was the first Chief Justice at Fort William (1774).

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Charter Act of 1833 — Company retained all commercial functions
Charter Act of 1793 — Monopoly extended for 20 years
Charter Act of 1813 — Education grant of one lakh rupees annually
Charter Act of 1853 — Territories held in trust
x: The Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company's commercial functions and made it a purely administrative body.

s:
Arrange in chronological order:
1. Pitt's India Act
2. Charter Act of 1793
3. Regulating Act
4. Charter Act of 1813
x: Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Act 1793, Charter Act 1813.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1793, to what were the salaries of the Board of Control charged?
x: The Charter Act of 1793 charged the Board of Control's salaries to Indian revenues and increased the Governor-General's control over Bombay and Madras.

s: What did the Charter Act of 1833, the final step towards centralisation, make the East India Company?
o: A trading body with its monopoly restored
A Crown department under the India Office
x: The 1833 Act ended the Company's commercial functions and made it purely administrative, while centralising legislation in the Governor-General-in-Council.

s: How many legislative members did the Charter Act of 1853 add to the Governor-General's Council?
x: The 1853 Act added six legislative members, separating legislative from executive functions of the Council.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1853, how were the Company's territories held?
o: For a fixed period of twenty years only
As independent territories under the Governor-General
As permanent private property of the Court of Directors
In trust for the Crown until Parliament otherwise provided
x: The Act declared that the territories were held in trust for Her Majesty until Parliament otherwise provided.

s: The Law Commission headed by Macaulay, regarded as the origin of the present Law Ministry, was set up under which Act?
x: The Charter Act of 1833 (Saint Helena Act) created a Law Commission under Macaulay, the origin of the Law Ministry. The Regulating Act 1773 set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta, the 1813 Act admitted missionaries and gave Rs 1 lakh for education, and the 1853 Act separated the legislative and executive functions of the GG's Council.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Indians' share in administration?
o: The Charter Act of 1833 said no Indian would be debarred from office by religion, birth, descent or colour.
The Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition for the civil services.
The Macaulay Committee (1854) was set up to give effect to open competition.
The Charter Act of 1833 put open competition into actual operation.
x: The 1833 Act only attempted open competition, which was not implemented; open competition came with the 1853 Act.

s: Which one of the following was the last Charter Act enacted by the British Parliament for the East India Company?
x: The Charter Act of 1853 was the last Charter Act. The Government of India Act, 1858 subsequently transferred the governance of India from the East India Company to the Crown.

s:
Assertion (A): The Charter Act, 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.
Reason (R): Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Charter Act, 1833 created the post of Governor-General of India, and Bentinck merely happened to be its first holder.

s: Which of the following about the Charter Act, 1813 is INCORRECT?
o: It permitted Christian missionaries to work in India.
It completely abolished the Company's trade monopoly in India.
It retained the Company's monopoly over the tea and China trade.
It provided an annual grant of ₹1 lakh for education.
x: The 1813 Act ended the Company's monopoly only partly, keeping the tea and China trade; complete abolition came in 1833.

s: Which Act completely abolished the Company's trade monopoly in India?
x: The Charter Act, 1833 ended the Company's trade monopoly completely and made it a purely administrative body. The 1813 Act ended it only partly, keeping tea and China trade.

s: Which British Act created the office of Governor-General of India and added a Law Member to the Governor-General’s Council?
x: The Charter Act, 1833 created the office of Governor-General of India and added a Law Member (Macaulay) to the Council. The 1853 Act separated legislative and executive functions.

s: Which Act provided an annual grant of Rs 1 lakh for education in India?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 provided the annual education grant of Rs 1 lakh.

s: By how many years did the Charter Act of 1793 extend the Company's trade monopoly?
x: The Charter Act of 1793 extended the monopoly by 20 years.

s: Which Charter Act allowed Christian missionaries to come to India?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 allowed Christian missionaries, after efforts by Charles Grant and Wilberforce.

s: Which Act separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council?
x: The Charter Act of 1853 separated the council's legislative and executive functions and added 6 legislative members.

s: Which body worked out the open competition for the civil services put into operation by the 1853 Act?
x: The 1853 Act put open competition into operation, and the Macaulay Committee of 1854 worked it out.

s: Which Section of the Charter Act, 1833 said no Indian would be debarred from office by religion, birth, descent or colour?
x: Section 87 of the 1833 Act laid this down, though open competition was only attempted then.

s: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly except in which of the following?
x: The 1813 Act did not end the monopoly completely: tea and the China trade remained exceptions. It also permitted missionaries to enter India.

s: Who was the first Law Member of the Governor-General's Council?
x: Macaulay became the first Law Member under the 1833 Act, not Impey; S.P. Sinha was the first Indian Law Member (1909).

s: Who was the last Governor-General of Bengal and the first Governor-General of India?
x: Under the Charter Act of 1833, William Bentinck, the last Governor-General of Bengal, became the first Governor-General of India.

s: Which Charter Act first asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's territories in India?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 asserted Crown sovereignty over the Company's territories, besides ending its monopoly except tea and China trade.

s: Which Act created the office of 'Governor-General of India'?
x: The Charter Act of 1833 created the Governor-General of India; Pitt's India Act brought dual control and the 1813 Act largely ended the Company's trade monopoly.

s: In which year was the Simon Commission, chaired by Sir John Simon, appointed?
x: The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927, two years before the scheduled review; all seven members were British and it was boycotted in India.

s: Which Act created the office of the High Commissioner for India in London?
x: The 1919 Act provided for a High Commissioner for India in London, a Public Service Commission and separate provincial budgets.

s: In which year did Montagu make his 20 August declaration on the gradual introduction of responsible government in India?
x: Montagu's declaration of 20 August 1917 formed the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1919, what was the upper house of the central legislature?
x: The 1919 Act made the Centre bicameral: the Council of State (upper) and the Legislative Assembly (lower).

s: In which Act was the term 'responsible government' used for the first time?
x: The 1919 Act first used the term 'responsible government'; it also made the Central Legislature bicameral and introduced provincial dyarchy.

s: Who was the first Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes?
x: Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner was the first Chancellor of the 120-member Chamber of Princes created under the 1919 Act.

s: Under provincial dyarchy (1919), with whom did the Governor administer the transferred subjects?
x: Transferred subjects were under the Governor and popular Ministers; reserved subjects were under the Governor and Executive Council.

s: In which year was the Public Accounts Committee first set up?
x: The PAC was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919.

s: To which communities did the Government of India Act, 1919 extend communal representation?
o: Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans
x: The 1919 Act extended it to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; the 1935 Act added depressed classes, women and labour.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1919:
1. It provided for direct elections.
2. Its franchise was based on adult suffrage.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 1919 Act brought direct elections, but on a limited franchise of property, tax and education, not adult suffrage.

s: The Government of India Act, 1919 provided for a statutory commission after how many years?
x: The Act provided for a commission after 10 years; the Simon Commission came in 1927, two years early.

s: On which date was the Public Service Commission provided by the 1919 Act set up?
x: The PSC was set up on 1 October 1926; 1 October 1937 was the Federal Court and 1 April 1935 the RBI.

s: The Simon Commission, boycotted with 'Simon Go Back', consisted of how many members?
x: The Simon Commission had 7 members, all British, chaired by Sir John Simon.

s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of reserved subjects under the provincial dyarchy introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919?
x: Police, finance and land revenue were reserved subjects administered by the Governor with the assistance of the Executive Council. Education, agriculture, public health and local self-government were transferred subjects.

s: Who were the Secretary of State for India and the Viceroy, respectively, at the time of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms?
x: Edwin Montagu was Secretary of State and Lord Chelmsford was Viceroy; their 1918 report led to the 1919 Act.

s: In which year was the Montagu-Chelmsford Report published?
x: The Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) followed Montagu's declaration of 20 August 1917 and formed the basis of the 1919 Act.

s: Which Act separated the central and provincial budgets for the first time?
x: The Government of India Act, 1919 separated the central and provincial budgets and defined Central and Provincial lists.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1919, how many of the six members of the Viceroy's Executive Council were to be Indians?
x: The 1919 Act required three of the six members of the Viceroy's Executive Council to be Indians.

s: Under the Government of India Act, 1858, through whom were the Crown's powers over India exercised?
x: The 1858 Act vested the Crown's powers in the Secretary of State for India, assisted by a 15-member Council of India; the Board of Control and Court of Directors were abolished.

s: Which Act transferred the rule of India from the Company to the British Crown?
x: The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred rule from the Company to the Crown and made the Governor-General the Viceroy. The 1861 and 1919 Acts reformed councils; 1947 ended British rule.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Government of India Act, 1919 – Bicameralism at the Centre
Indian Councils Act, 1909 – Transferred rule from the Company to the Crown
Government of India Act, 1935 – Federal Court (1937)
Government of India Act, 1858 – Transferred rule from the Company to the Crown
x: The 1909 Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims; it was the 1858 Act that transferred rule to the Crown.

s: In which year was the Court of Directors of the East India Company abolished?
x: The Court of Directors lasted till 1858, when the Government of India Act abolished it; the Regulating Act did not abolish it.

s: How many members did the Council of India, created in 1858 to assist the Secretary of State, have?
x: The 1858 Act created the Secretary of State for India with a 15-member Council of India.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1858:
1. It abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors.
2. It created the office of Secretary of State for India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the 1858 Act abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors and created the Secretary of State for India.

s: Who was the first Viceroy of India?
x: The Government of India Act, 1858 styled the Governor-General also as Viceroy; Lord Canning was the first.

s: Who was the last Viceroy of India?
x: Lord Canning was the first Viceroy (1858) and Lord Mountbatten the last.

s: Which Act styled the Governor-General also as 'Viceroy'?
x: The 1858 Act made the Governor-General also the Viceroy, Lord Canning being the first.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Regulating Act, 1773?
o: It abolished the Court of Directors.
It made the Presidencies of Bombay and Madras subordinate to Bengal.
It was based on the report of a committee under Lord North.
It was the British Parliament's first step to control the East India Company.
x: The Regulating Act did not abolish the Court of Directors, which survived until the 1858 Act.

s: What mainly made the British Parliament intervene in the Company's affairs in Bengal in 1772?
o: The appointment of the first Viceroy
The Carnatic Wars and the Mysore conflict
The famine, falling revenue and the Company's financial crisis
The transfer of Bombay and Madras to Parliament
x: The Bengal famine, declining revenue and the Company's financial crisis compelled Parliament to intervene in 1772.

s: The Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) initially had one Chief Justice and how many other judges?
x: It had one Chief Justice (Sir Elijah Impey) and three other judges.

s: Which Act banned private trade and the acceptance of bribes by Company officials?
x: The Regulating Act, 1773 banned both private trade and bribes by Company officials.

s: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774)?
x: Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court set up in 1774; Gwyer was the first Chief Justice of the Federal Court (1937).

s: Who headed the committee whose report led to the Regulating Act, 1773?
x: The Lord North committee report led to the Regulating Act, 1773.

s: By what name is the Amending Act of 1781, which separated judicial and executive functions, also known?
x: The Amending Act 1781 is the Act of Settlement; the Saint Helena Act is the Charter Act of 1833.

s: Under which Act was the Supreme Court at Calcutta (Fort William) established?
x: The Regulating Act, 1773 provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta, set up in 1774 with Sir Elijah Impey as first Chief Justice.

s: Under the Act of 1767, how much was the East India Company to pay the British Government every year?
x: The Act of 1767 required the Company to pay £400,000 a year to the British Government.

s: Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal?
x: The Regulating Act, 1773 made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal; Warren Hastings was the first.

s: How did Pitt's India Act, 1784 describe the Company's territories in India?
x: The Act described the territories as British possessions in India and made the Company subordinate to the State.

s: Besides overriding his Council, what did the Act of 1786 empower the Governor-General to do?
x: The Act of 1786 gave the Governor-General two separate powers: to override his Council and to act as Commander-in-Chief.

s: Under the Dual Control set up by Pitt's India Act, 1784, to which body were political affairs assigned?
x: Dual Control gave political functions to the Board of Control and commercial functions to the Court of Directors.

s: Which Act set up the Board of Control?
x: Pitt's India Act, 1784 set up the Board of Control for political affairs, beside the Court of Directors for commercial affairs.

s: How many members did the Board of Control under Pitt's India Act have?
x: The Board of Control had 6 members, including a Secretary of State and the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

s: To how many members did Pitt's India Act, 1784 reduce the Governor-General's council?
x: Pitt's India Act cut the council to 3, from the 4 members given by the Regulating Act.

s: Under the Regulating Act, 1773, how many members did the Executive Council assisting the Governor-General of Bengal have?
x: The Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings) had a four-member Executive Council; Pitt's India Act later reduced it to three.

s: By the Act of which year was the Governor-General's power to override his Council first given to Lord Cornwallis?
x: The Act of 1786 gave the override power to Cornwallis; the Charter Act of 1793 extended it to all future Governors-General and Presidency Governors.

s: Which Act introduced 'Dual Control'?
x: Pitt's India Act, 1784 introduced Dual Control; the Regulating Act set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta.

s: Which Act introduced dual control?
x: Pitt's India Act, 1784 introduced dual control; the Charter Act of 1833 created the Governor-General of India.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Act)
a. Regulating Act, 1773
b. Charter Act, 1813
c. Government of India Act, 1858
d. Indian Independence Act, 1947
List-II (Provision)
1. Ended Company rule
2. Partitioned India into India and Pakistan
3. First Supreme Court
4. Mostly ended the Company's trade monopoly
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: 1773 set up the first Supreme Court; 1813 mostly ended the trade monopoly; 1858 ended Company rule; 1947 partitioned India.

s: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1892, on the recommendation of which of the following bodies were nominations to the councils made?
x: The 1892 Act's indirect system worked through recommendations from universities, municipalities and chambers of commerce.

s: Who among the following was NOT one of the first three Indians nominated by Canning to the expanded legislative council?
x: The first three Indians nominated by Canning were the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was not one of these three nominees.

s: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, for how long at most could an ordinance issued by the Viceroy remain in force?
x: An ordinance under the 1861 Act lasted at most six months, not twelve.

s: Who among the following particularly criticised the absence of Indians in the legislative council as a lesson of the Revolt of 1857?
x: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan attributed part of the crisis to the absence of Indian opinion in the council, a concern addressed through later expansion and nomination of Indian members.

s: Under which Act were the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras set up in 1862?
x: The Indian High Courts Act was passed in 1861 and the three High Courts were set up under it in 1862.

s: Which Act restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras?
x: The Indian Councils Act, 1861 restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras; separate electorates came only in 1909.

s: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1892, which of the following could the legislative councils do?
o: Discuss the budget but not vote on it
Not discuss the budget at all
x: The 1892 Act allowed discussion of the budget without a vote; supplementary questions came only in 1909.

s: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1892, how many days' notice did questions in the councils require?
x: Questions needed 6 days' notice, and no supplementary questions were allowed.

s: Which of the following was NOT a feature of the Indian Councils Act, 1861?
o: It gave statutory recognition to the portfolio system.
It gave the Viceroy an ordinance power of up to six months.
It restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras.
It began indirect election to the councils.
x: Indirect election began only with the Indian Councils Act, 1892.

s: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1909, to how many were the additional members of the Central Legislative Council raised?
x: The 1909 Act raised the additional members to 60 (total 69), though the Centre kept an official majority.

s: At the time of the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909), which posts did Morley and Minto respectively hold?
o: Governor of Bombay and Secretary of State
Secretary of State and Governor of Bengal
x: John Morley was Secretary of State for India and Lord Minto was the Viceroy when the Indian Councils Act, 1909 was passed.

s: Who is known as the 'Father of Communal Electorate'?
x: Lord Minto, of the Morley-Minto reforms (Indian Councils Act, 1909), which introduced separate electorates for Muslims.

s: Who became the first Indian Law Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council after the 1909 Act?
x: The 1909 Act first brought Indians into the Viceroy's and Governors' Executive Councils, and S.P. Sinha became the first Indian Law Member.

s: Which Act first allowed supplementary questions in the legislative councils?
x: The 1892 Act allowed no supplementary questions; the 1909 Act allowed them.

s: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1909, what was the total strength of the Central Legislative Council?
x: Additional members rose to 60, making a total of 69 (37 officials and 32 non-officials).

s: Which Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims?
x: The Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act, 1909) gave Muslims a separate electorate; Lord Minto is called the Father of Communal Electorate.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Councils Act, 1909:
1. It kept an official majority in the Central Legislative Council.
2. It allowed a non-official majority in the provincial councils.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 1909 Act kept an official majority at the Centre but allowed a non-official majority in the provinces.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Satyendra Prasad Sinha – First Indian on the Viceroy's Executive Council
Government of India Act, 1919 – Chamber of Princes
Government of India Act, 1935 – Maurice Gwyer as Chief Justice of the Federal Court
Indian Councils Act, 1909 – Established the Chamber of Princes
x: The Chamber of Princes was set up under the 1919 Act; the 1909 Act allowed supplementary questions.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Charter Act, 1833 added a Law Member and ended the Company's commercial activities.
The Indian Councils Act, 1892 permitted budget discussion and limited indirect election.
The Morley-Minto Reforms introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred power to the British Crown.
x: C is incorrect: provincial dyarchy came with the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919), not the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909), which brought separate electorates. The other three statements are correct.

s: Who was the first Governor-General of India?
x: William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833; Canning was the first Viceroy and Hastings the first Governor-General of Bengal.

s: Which of the following designation – first holder pairs is correctly matched?
x: Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India (1833); Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal and Canning the first Viceroy.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Designation)
A. Governor-General of Bengal
B. Governor-General of India
C. Viceroy
List-II (Act)
1. Charter Act, 1833
2. Regulating Act, 1773
3. Government of India Act, 1858
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: GG of Bengal came by the Regulating Act 1773, GG of India by the Charter Act 1833, and the Viceroy title by the GoI Act 1858.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Government of India Act, 1858 ended Company rule.
The Indian Councils Act, 1861 associated Indians with legislative councils.
The Government of India Act, 1858 introduced dyarchy in provinces.
The Charter Act, 1853 was the last Charter Act.
x: Option C is incorrect: dyarchy in the provinces came with the Government of India Act, 1919, not 1858. The 1858 Act ended Company rule, and the other statements are right.

s: Sir B.N. Rau, who prepared the initial draft of the Constitution, later served as a judge of which court?
x: B.N. Rau prepared the initial draft and later served as a judge of the International Court of Justice.

s: Who illuminated the original Preamble of the Constitution?
x: The original Preamble was illuminated by Beohar Rammanohar Sinha. This is distinct from the persons associated with handwriting or other artwork in the original Constitution.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the Constituent Assembly is wrongly matched?
o: Speaker when sitting as Dominion Legislature – G.V. Mavalankar
x: The Constitutional Adviser was B.N. Rau; Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary President.

s: Who was the first permanent Vice-President of the Constituent Assembly?
x: H.C. Mukherjee was the first permanent Vice-President; Sinha was the temporary President and Prasad the permanent President from 11 December 1946.

s: Which one of the following was NOT a member of the seven-member Drafting Committee?
x: The Drafting Committee included Ambedkar, N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, K.M. Munshi, Saadullah, N. Madhava Rau and T.T. Krishnamachari. J.B. Kripalani chaired the Fundamental Rights Sub-committee and was not a member of the Drafting Committee.

s: Who were the two Vice-Presidents of the Constituent Assembly?
x: H.C. Mukherjee and V.T. Krishnamachari served as the Vice-Presidents of the Constituent Assembly.

s:
Assertion (A): B.L. Mitter was later replaced by N. Madhava Rao on the Drafting Committee.
Reason (R): D.P. Khaitan was later replaced by T.T. Krishnamachari on the Drafting Committee.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true but unrelated: B.L. Mitter was replaced by N. Madhava Rao and D.P. Khaitan by T.T. Krishnamachari. One replacement does not explain the other.

s: Dr Sachchidananda Sinha was made temporary President as the eldest member, following the practice of which country?
x: Sinha became temporary President as the eldest member, following French practice.

s: Who sketched the National Emblem in the original Constitution of India?
x: Dinanath Bhargava sketched the National Emblem under Nandalal Bose, who led the illustrations.

s: Who wrote the calligraphy of the original Constitution of India?
x: The calligraphy of the original Constitution was done by Prem Behari Narain Raizada.

s: Who led the work of illustrating the original Constitution of India?
x: Nandalal Bose led the illustrations; Dinanath Bhargava, under him, sketched the National Emblem.

s: How many members did the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly have?
x: The Drafting Committee, set up on 29 August 1947 under Ambedkar, had seven members.

s: Who presided over the Constituent Assembly when it functioned as the constitution-making body and who presided over it as the legislature, respectively?
o: G.V. Mavalankar and Dr Rajendra Prasad
Dr B.R. Ambedkar and G.V. Mavalankar
Jawaharlal Nehru and Dr Rajendra Prasad
Dr Rajendra Prasad and G.V. Mavalankar
x: Dr Rajendra Prasad chaired the Assembly in its constitution-making capacity, whereas G.V. Mavalankar presided over it when it functioned as the legislature.

s: For how many days did the Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar, sit?
x: The seven-member Drafting Committee chaired by Ambedkar sat for 141 days.

s: When were the elections to the Constituent Assembly held?
x: The elections were held in July–August 1946, not June–July; the provincial assembly elections had been held in January 1946.

s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Publication of the Draft Constitution
B. Adoption of the Objectives Resolution
C. Beginning of the third reading of the Constitution
D. Setting up of the Drafting Committee
x: The Objectives Resolution was adopted on 22 January 1947, the Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947, the Draft Constitution was published on 21 February 1948, and the third reading began on 14 November 1949.

s: On which date was Dr Rajendra Prasad elected President of the Constituent Assembly?
x: Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946. The first meeting on 9 December 1946 had 207 members and was boycotted by the Muslim League.

s: On which date was the Draft Constitution published?
x: The Draft Constitution was published on 21 February 1948; 22 January 1947 was the adoption of the Objectives Resolution.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the Constituent Assembly is wrongly matched?
o: Adoption of the National Flag – 22 July 1947
Adoption of the Munshi-Ayyangar formula – 14 September 1949
Election of Rajendra Prasad as first President – 24 January 1950
x: Commonwealth membership was ratified in May 1949; 14 September 1949 is when the Munshi-Ayyangar formula was adopted.

s: Which of the following provisions came into force on 26 November 1949?
x: Citizenship, elections, the provisional Parliament and transitional provisions came into force on 26 November 1949; the rest commenced on 26 January 1950.

s: How many members attended the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1946?
x: 207 members, including nine women, attended; the Muslim League boycotted the meeting.

s: On which date did the Constituent Assembly adopt the National Flag?
x: The National Flag was adopted on 22 July 1947; 22 January 1947 was the adoption of the Objectives Resolution.

s: What was adopted at the final meeting of the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950?
x: At its final meeting on 24 January 1950 the Constituent Assembly adopted the National Anthem (and elected Rajendra Prasad President). The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and the flag on 22 July 1947.

s: On which date was Dr Rajendra Prasad elected the first President of India at the Assembly's meeting?
x: At the final meeting on 24 January 1950 Prasad was elected first President; on 11 December 1946 he had been elected President of the Assembly.

s: In which year was the Constitution of India adopted and enacted by the Constituent Assembly?
x: The Constitution was adopted and enacted on 26 November 1949, at the eleventh session; it came into force on 26 January 1950.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949.
2. The Constitution of India came into force on 24 January 1950.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: It was adopted on 26 November 1949; 24 January 1950 was the day members signed it. It came into force on 26 January 1950.

s: Why was 26 January chosen as the date of commencement of the Constitution of India?
o: It was the date of the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly
It was the date of the Objectives Resolution
It was the date the Indian Independence Act received royal assent
It was the date of Purna Swaraj observed from 1930
x: 26 January was the Purna Swaraj day (Lahore Congress 1929, observed from 1930), so the Republic began on 26 January 1950.

s: On which date was the Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent Assembly?
x: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946; it was adopted on 22 January 1947.

s: Which part of the Constitution of India is based on the Objectives Resolution adopted on 22 January 1947?
x: The Objectives Resolution, adopted unanimously on 22 January 1947, became the basis of the Preamble.

s: On which date did the Constituent Assembly first meet as the Dominion Legislature, with G.V. Mavalankar as Speaker?
x: The Assembly first met as the Dominion Legislature on 17 November 1947, with Mavalankar as Speaker.

s: Hindi Diwas (14 September) marks the adoption of which of the following in the Constituent Assembly in 1949?
x: The Munshi-Ayyangar formula on official language was adopted on 14 September 1949, now observed as Hindi Diwas.

s: Where was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held on 9 December 1946?
o: Constitution Hall (now Central Hall), New Delhi
x: The first meeting was held in the Constitution Hall, now the Central Hall of Parliament, New Delhi.

s: Since which year has Constitution Day (26 November) been observed?
x: Constitution Day has been observed since 2015, the 125th birth-anniversary year of B.R. Ambedkar.

s: Why did the strength of the Constituent Assembly decline from 389 to 299?
o: the nominated members resigned before the commencement of the Constitution
members representing the areas that became part of Pakistan withdrew from the Assembly
the British Government dissolved the provincial representation
the princely states refused to send their representatives
x: The representatives from the territories that went to Pakistan withdrew from the Constituent Assembly, reducing its strength from 389 to 299.

s: From which Act did the restricted franchise used in electing the Constituent Assembly come?
x: The election used the restricted franchise of the 1935 Act, based on tax, education and property qualifications.

s: Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, what was to be the total strength of the Constituent Assembly?
x: The total strength was 389: 296 from British India and 93 from the princely states.

s: How were the representatives of the princely States in the Constituent Assembly chosen?
o: Elected by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies
x: Princely representatives were nominated by the rulers; only the provincial members were elected by the Provincial Assemblies.

s: Which of the following describes the nature of the Constituent Assembly of India?
o: Wholly nominated by the British Government
Wholly nominated by the princely rulers
x: The Assembly was partly elected and partly nominated; it was not based on adult franchise.

s: How were the members of the Constituent Assembly from the provinces chosen?
o: Indirectly elected by Provincial Assembly members by proportional representation (single transferable vote)
x: Each community's members in the Provincial Assembly elected their representatives by proportional representation with single transferable vote; there was no adult franchise.

s: How many seats did the Muslim League win in the 1946 Constituent Assembly election?
x: The Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League 73 and others 15.

s: How many seats were allotted to the Princely States in the Constituent Assembly?
x: Of the 389 planned seats, 296 were for British India and 93 for the Princely States.

s: On which date did representatives of princely states first take their seats in the Constituent Assembly, in its third session?
x: States such as Baroda, Bikaner, Jaipur, Patiala, Rewa and Udaipur joined from the third session on 28 April 1947.

s: From which province was Dr B.R. Ambedkar first elected to the Constituent Assembly?
x: Ambedkar was first elected from East Bengal; later he was elected from the Bombay seat vacated by M.R. Jayakar.

s: Out of the 389 seats planned for the Constituent Assembly, how many were allotted to British India?
x: British India got 296 seats (292 Governor's provinces + 4 Chief Commissioners' provinces); the princely states got 93.

s: Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, seats in the Constituent Assembly were allotted in what ratio to population?
x: Seats were allotted roughly one member per 10 lakh (one million) population.

s: Whose vacated seat from Bombay did Dr B.R. Ambedkar fill when he re-entered the Constituent Assembly?
x: Ambedkar was first elected from East Bengal and later from the Bombay seat vacated by M.R. Jayakar.

s: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the Munshi-Ayyangar formula?
o: Continuation of English during the transition
Inclusion of 14 languages in the Eighth Schedule
Immediate discontinuation of English for Union purposes
x: The formula provided for a 15-year transition, continued English for Union and inter-provincial use meanwhile, and listed 14 other languages. It did not provide for immediate discontinuation of English.

s: On 24 January 1950, which song was declared the national song of India and accorded equal honour with the National Anthem?
x: Rajendra Prasad declared Vande Mataram the national song on 24 January 1950 and stated that it would be honoured equally with the National Anthem.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the constitutional position of national symbols?
o: Article 51A(a) refers to respect for the National Flag and the National Anthem.
Article 51A(a) is part of the Fundamental Duties.
A 2026 amendment gave the National Song statutory protection comparable to the Anthem.
Article 51A(a) expressly names the National Song along with the Flag and the Anthem.
x: Article 51A(a) names the National Flag and the National Anthem, not the National Song.

s: In which language was Vande Mataram, declared the national song, originally composed?
x: Bankimchandra's Vande Mataram was in Sanskrit, written in Bengali script.

s: Article 51A(a) names which national symbols for citizens to respect?
o: The National Anthem and the National Song
The National Song and the National Flag
The National Flag and the National Anthem
The National Flag, Anthem and Song
x: Article 51A(a) names the Flag and the Anthem, not the National Song.

s: About how long does the full rendition of the National Anthem take?
x: The full rendition of Jana Gana Mana takes about 52 seconds.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that students who stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem could not be punished?
o: Bijoe Emmanuel v State of Kerala
Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
x: In Bijoe Emmanuel v State of Kerala (1986) the Court protected students who stood respectfully but did not sing.

s: Who were the members of the Cabinet Mission that proposed the scheme for forming the Constituent Assembly?
o: Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander
A.V. Alexander, Rajendra Prasad and Stafford Cripps
x: The Cabinet Mission consisted of Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander. It arrived in India in 1946 to work out the constitutional and political arrangements.

s: Through which of the following did the British accept the principle of a Constituent Assembly in 1940?
x: The August Offer of 1940 accepted the principle; Nehru's clear statement of support had come in 1938.

s: Which of the following made the proposal for an elected Constituent Assembly in 1942?
x: The Cripps Mission of 1942 proposed an elected Constituent Assembly; the Assembly was actually constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.

s: Where did the Swaraj Party make the first formal demand for a Constituent Assembly in May 1934?
x: The Swaraj Party's first formal demand came at Ranchi in May 1934; the Congress adopted it at Patna.

s: In which year did Nehru make a clear statement of support for a Constituent Assembly?
x: Nehru's clear statement came in 1938; the August Offer accepted the principle in 1940.

s: When did the Cabinet Mission arrive in India?
x: The Cabinet Mission of Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps and Alexander arrived on 24 March 1946.

s: With which of the following is M.N. Roy associated in India's constitutional history?
o: First putting forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly
Preparing the first draft of the Constitution
x: M.N. Roy first put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India in 1934.

s: When did the Indian National Congress make its first official demand for a Constituent Assembly?
x: The Congress Working Committee's resolution of June 1934 was the Congress's first official demand for a Constituent Assembly.

s: Which document of 1895 made the first explicit demand for Fundamental Rights in India?
x: The Constitution of India Bill (1895) was the first explicit demand for Fundamental Rights.

s: Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) was called by the Muslim League primarily to:
o: Press its demand for Pakistan after withdrawing its acceptance of the Cabinet Mission Plan
Oppose the adoption of Hindi as the official language
Protest the ratification of India's Commonwealth membership
Protest the election of Rajendra Prasad as President
x: The Muslim League called Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946 to press for Pakistan after it withdrew from the Cabinet Mission Plan. It led to the Calcutta riots.

s: Which portfolio did Sardar Patel hold in the Interim Government?
x: Patel held Home, Information and Broadcasting; Nehru had External Affairs, Liaquat Ali Khan Finance and Rajendra Prasad Food and Agriculture.

s: Which portfolio did Liaquat Ali Khan hold in the Interim Government of 1946?
x: Liaquat Ali Khan held Finance; Home (with Information and Broadcasting) was with Sardar Patel and Food and Agriculture with Rajendra Prasad.

s: On which date did the Interim Government of 1946 take charge?
x: It was announced on 24 August 1946 and took charge on 2 September 1946.

s: Who held the Law portfolio in the Interim Government of 1946?
x: Jogendra Nath Mandal (League) held Law; Ambedkar later became the first Law Minister of independent India.

s: Who held the Defence portfolio in the Interim Government of 1946?
x: Baldev Singh held Defence; Patel held Home, Jagjivan Ram Labour and Rajagopalachari Education.

s: Who was the first Law Minister of independent India?
x: Ambedkar was the first Law Minister of independent India; J.N. Mandal held Law in the Interim Government.

s: Who was the ex-officio President of the Executive Council in the Interim Government of 1946?
x: The Viceroy was ex-officio President of the Executive Council; Nehru was its Vice-President.

s: When did the Muslim League join the Interim Government formed in 1946?
x: The Interim Government took charge on 2 September 1946; the Muslim League joined it in October 1946.

s: Which portfolio did Jawaharlal Nehru hold in the Interim Government of 1946?
x: Nehru held External Affairs and Commonwealth Relations and was Vice-President of the Executive Council.

s: Which portfolio did C. Rajagopalachari hold in the Interim Government of 1946?
x: C. Rajagopalachari held Education and Arts in the Interim Government.

s: How many of the 299 members signed the Constitution on 24 January 1950?
x: 284 of the 299 members signed the Constitution at the final session on 24 January 1950.

s: How many Articles and Schedules did the first draft of the Constitution prepared by B.N. Rau contain?
x: B.N. Rau, the Constitutional Advisor, prepared the first draft of 243 Articles and 13 Schedules.

s: For how many days in all did the Constituent Assembly sit?
x: The Assembly held 11 sessions over 165 days; the Draft Constitution alone was discussed for 114 days.

s: The Draft Constitution initially contained how many Articles?
x: The Draft had 315 Articles; 395 Articles belong to the adopted text.

s: How many amendments to the Draft Constitution were proposed in the Constituent Assembly?
x: 7,635 amendments were proposed, of which 2,473 were discussed.

s: For how many days was the Draft Constitution considered by the Assembly?
x: The Draft was considered for 114 days; the Drafting Committee sat 141 days and the Assembly 165 days in all.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Constituent Assembly:
1. It took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to frame the Constitution.
2. It sat for 141 days in all.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Assembly sat for 165 days in 11 sessions; 141 days is the number of days the Drafting Committee sat.

s: How many Articles, Parts and Schedules did the Constitution of India have when it was adopted?
x: The original Constitution had 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Draft Constitution contained 315 Articles.
2. The original Constitution of India had 12 Schedules.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Draft had 315 Articles; the original Constitution had 395 Articles and 8 Schedules (12 Schedules is today's number).

s: In how many sessions did the Constituent Assembly complete the framing of the Constitution?
x: The Assembly framed the Constitution in 11 sessions over 165 sitting days; the 24 January 1950 meeting made 12 in all.

s: The Constituent Assembly is said to have taken 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to frame the Constitution. This period is counted between which two dates?
x: From the first meeting on 9 December 1946 to adoption on 26 November 1949 is 2 years, 11 months and 18 days.

s: Who chaired the Minorities Sub-committee of the Constituent Assembly?
x: H.C. Mukherjee chaired the Minorities Sub-committee; Kripalani chaired the Fundamental Rights Sub-committee.

s: Who chaired the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal Areas?
x: Sardar Patel chaired the Advisory Committee; J.B. Kripalani chaired the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee.

s: What did the Union Powers Committee of the Constituent Assembly deal with?
x: The Union Powers Committee handled the distribution of federal subjects; the Order of Business Committee handled the daily agenda.

s: Who chaired the 1931 Karachi Congress Flag Committee?
x: Patel chaired the 1931 Karachi Congress Flag Committee. Rajendra Prasad chaired the separate 1947 Constituent Assembly Flag Committee.

s: Which of the following committee – chairman pairs is correctly matched?
o: Order of Business Committee – H.C. Mukherjee
x: Patel chaired the Provincial Constitution Committee; H.C. Mukherjee the Minorities Sub-Committee, Nehru the States Committee and Munshi the Order of Business Committee.

s: Which of the following committee – chairman pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribals – Sardar Patel
x: The Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee was chaired by J.B. Kripalani, not H.C. Mukherjee; Patel chaired the Advisory and Provincial Constitution Committees.

s: Who chaired the Steering Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
x: Prasad chaired the Steering Committee; 'Steering Committee – Nehru' was the wrong pair in APPSC Group 1, 2004.

s: Who chaired the States Committee, for negotiating with the princely states?
x: Nehru chaired the States Committee, as well as the Union Constitution and Union Powers Committees.

s: Who chaired the Order of Business Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
x: K.M. Munshi chaired the Order of Business Committee; Pattabhi Sitaramayya chaired the House Committee.

s: Who chaired both the Union Constitution Committee and the Union Powers Committee?
x: Nehru chaired both committees, which dealt with the Union's structure and the division of legislative power.

s: Who chaired the North-East Frontier Tribal and Assam Excluded Areas Sub-Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
x: Gopinath Bardoloi chaired the NE Frontier Tribal and Assam Excluded Areas sub-committee; A.V. Thakkar chaired the one for other excluded areas.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Committee)
A. Steering Committee
B. Union Powers Committee
C. Provincial Constitution Committee
D. Order of Business Committee
List-II (Chairman)
1. K.M. Munshi
2. Sardar Patel
3. Jawaharlal Nehru
4. Rajendra Prasad
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Prasad chaired the Steering Committee, Nehru the Union Powers Committee, Patel the Provincial Constitution Committee and K.M. Munshi the Order of Business Committee.

s: Who chaired the House Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
x: B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya chaired the House Committee.

s: Who chaired the Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (other than Assam) Sub-Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
x: A.V. Thakkar chaired this sub-committee; Gopinath Bardoloi chaired the one for the North-East and Assam.

s: Until when did the Provisional Parliament function before the first Lok Sabha?
x: After 26 January 1950 the Assembly worked as the Provisional Parliament until 17 April 1952, after the 1951-52 elections.

s: Which of the following correctly describes India's status on 15 August 1947?
o: A sovereign republic with no constitutional link to the Crown
A federation of independent princely states
A Dominion with the British monarch as nominal head
A colony governed directly by the British Parliament
x: India became a Dominion on 15 August 1947, with the British monarch as its nominal head.

s: After independence, on whose advice was the Governor-General of each Dominion to act?
x: The Governor-General, common or separate for each Dominion, was to act on the advice of the Dominion ministers.

s: About how many princely states became theoretically free when paramountcy lapsed in 1947?
x: About 565 princely states were theoretically free after paramountcy lapsed, though they were expected to join India or Pakistan.

s: On which date did Kashmir accede to India?
x: Kashmir acceded to India on 26 October 1947 after the tribal invasion.

s: After the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the Constituent Assembly performed which of the following functions?
o: It functioned only as the provincial legislature of the newly formed Union
It functioned as the legislature of British India under the control of the Viceroy
It functioned only as the constitution-making body until 26 January 1950
It functioned both as a sovereign constitution-making body and as the Dominion legislature
x: The Act made the Constituent Assembly fully sovereign in its constitution-making role and also made it the Dominion legislature. The Central Legislative Assembly consequently ceased to function.

s: As what did the Constituent Assembly continue after 26 January 1950?
x: After the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, the Constituent Assembly functioned as the Provisional Parliament until the first general elections held in 1951–52.

s: The immediate historical significance of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 was that it
o: ended provincial autonomy and restored direct British rule over India
combined sovereignty with partition and enabled a quick transfer of power under dominion status
abolished the Constituent Assembly and transferred power to the princely States
created a unitary republic with universal adult franchise
x: The Act gave sovereignty to India in the context of partition. Congress accepted dominion status to facilitate a quick and peaceful transfer of power and to support a strong Centre.

s: Which Act ended British sovereignty over India and gave the Constituent Assembly legislative powers as well?
x: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 ended British sovereignty and gave the Constituent Assemblies both constitution-making and legislative powers.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Last Viceroy of India — C. Rajagopalachari
Last Governor-General of India — C. Rajagopalachari
First Governor-General of independent India — Lord Mountbatten
Last Viceroy of India — Lord Mountbatten
x: C. Rajagopalachari was the last Governor-General, not the last Viceroy. Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy and the first Governor-General of independent India.

s: On which date did the Indian Independence Bill receive royal assent?
x: The Bill was introduced in the Commons on 4 July 1947 and received royal assent on 18 July 1947.

s: On which date was the Indian Independence Bill introduced in the House of Commons?
x: It was introduced on 4 July 1947; royal assent followed on 18 July 1947.

s: On which plan was the Indian Independence Act, 1947 based?
x: The 3 June 1947 Plan of Mountbatten, accepted by the Congress and the League, was the basis of the Act.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Mountbatten Plan:
1. It was announced on 3 June 1947.
2. It was accepted by both the Congress and the Muslim League.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the 3 June 1947 Plan was accepted by the Congress and the League and became the basis of the Act.

s: Who chaired the Punjab and Bengal Boundary Commissions?
x: Radcliffe chaired both Boundary Commissions; the award was published on 17 August 1947.

s: On which date was the Radcliffe award published?
x: The award came out on 17 August 1947, two days after independence.

s: When did Hyderabad sign a Standstill Agreement with India?
x: Hyderabad signed a Standstill Agreement in November 1947; Kashmir acceded on 26 October 1947.

s: On which date did India's dominion status come to an end?
x: Dominion status ended when India became a Republic on 26 January 1950.

s: Who was the last and only Indian Governor-General of India?
x: Rajagopalachari was the last and only Indian Governor-General (June 1948-January 1950); Mountbatten was the first GG of independent India.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Independence Act, 1947:
1. The British Crown lost its veto.
2. The Central Legislative Assembly continued alongside the Constituent Assembly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Crown lost its veto, but the Central Legislative Assembly ended; the Constituent Assembly became the Dominion legislature.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the princely states in 1947?
o: Finance was ceded under the Instrument of Accession.
Defence was ceded under the Instrument of Accession.
Communications were ceded under the Instrument of Accession.
Hyderabad signed a Standstill Agreement in November 1947.
x: The Instrument of Accession ceded defence, external affairs and communications, not finance.

s: Under the Instrument of Accession (1947), a princely state ceded defence, external affairs and which other subject to the Dominion?
x: The Instrument of Accession ceded defence, external affairs and communications, not finance.

s: Which was the first law to receive the assent of C. Rajagopalachari as Governor-General?
x: As Governor-General, C. Rajagopalachari gave assent to the Madras Estates (Abolition) Act on 2 April 1949.

s: On which date did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar warn against the "grammar of anarchy" in his closing speech?
x: Ambedkar used the expression “grammar of anarchy” in his closing speech on 25 November 1949.

s: Critics who called the Indian Constitution a 'patchwork' meant that it was:
o: Drafted without any debate in the Constituent Assembly
Framed by a body elected on adult franchise
Largely borrowed from various other constitutions and sources
Written only by the British Parliament
x: The Constitution was called 'borrowed' or a 'patchwork' because it drew heavily on provisions from various constitutions and sources.

s: About how long did the Constituent Assembly take to complete its work?
x: The Assembly took about three years, for which it was criticised, along with not being based on adult franchise.

s: Who stated that constitutional morality “is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated”?
x: The statement was made by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar on 4 November 1948. The expression was borrowed from George Grote.

s: Who called the Constituent Assembly 'a body of Hindus'?
x: Viscount Simon called it 'a body of Hindus'; Granville Austin called it a one-party body in an essentially one-party country.

s: Critics said the Assembly took about 3 years, compared with about how long for the USA?
x: Critics called the Assembly time-consuming: about 3 years against about 4 months for the USA.

s: From whom did Ambedkar borrow his phrase on constitutional morality?
x: Ambedkar's 4 November 1948 remark that constitutional morality has to be cultivated was borrowed from George Grote.

s: Which of the following remarks is correctly matched with its speaker?
o: Delay adult franchise by 15 years – Rajendra Prasad
'A Constitution, like a machine, is a lifeless thing' – Rajendra Prasad
x: Prasad said this on 26 November 1949; 'Drifting Committee' was Naziruddin Ahmed's, 'a body of Hindus' Viscount Simon's, and Maulana Azad wanted adult franchise delayed.

s: Who called the Drafting Committee a 'Drifting Committee'?
x: Naziruddin Ahmed mocked the Drafting Committee as the 'Drifting Committee'.

s: Who said that the Constituent Assembly represented 'only one major community' in India?
x: Winston Churchill said the Assembly represented only one major community; Viscount Simon called it 'a body of Hindus'.

s: Before Indian independence, the Madras Assembly had resolved to divide the Presidency into which four units?
x: The Madras Assembly resolved to divide the Presidency into Andhra, Tamil, Karnataka and Kerala four months before independence.

s: In which year did the continuing demand for a separate Andhra ultimately result in the creation of Andhra State?
x: The Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee rejected linguistic States at the time, but the Andhra demand continued and resulted in the Andhra State of 1953.

s: Who chaired the Linguistic Provinces Commission, appointed on 17 June 1948?
x: The Linguistic Provinces Commission was chaired by S.K. Dar, a retired judge of the Allahabad High Court.

s: Which of the following is true of both the Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee?
o: Both accepted linguistic reorganisation without qualification
Both rejected linguistic States for the time being
Both recommended the immediate creation of Andhra State
Both dealt only with state boundaries
x: Both turned down linguistic States at that stage, though the JVP Committee left room for Andhra if public demand was strong.

s: Who did the 'P' in the JVP Committee stand for?
x: JVP stood for Jawaharlal, Vallabhbhai (Patel) and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.

s: On which date did Nehru accept the demand for an Andhra province?
x: Nehru accepted the Andhra demand on 27 November 1947, but Andhra was dropped from the Draft of 21 February 1948.

s: Who called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Indian Constitution?
x: Ambedkar called the DPSP a 'novel feature', replying that borrowed features were adapted to Indian conditions.

s: From which country had Ireland, from which India took the Directive Principles, itself taken the idea?
x: Ireland took the idea of Directive Principles from Spain; India adapted it as a novel feature of its Constitution.

s: From which country was the procedure for amendment of the Constitution (Article 368) borrowed?
x: The amendment procedure came from South Africa, not Ireland or France.

s: From which country was nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha borrowed?
x: Nomination to the Rajya Sabha came from Ireland; the election of its members came from South Africa.

s: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution was borrowed from South Africa?
o: Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha
Election of members of the Rajya Sabha
x: Election of Rajya Sabha members (and the amendment procedure) came from South Africa; nomination to the Rajya Sabha came from Ireland.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The method of election of members of the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from South Africa.
2. Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from Ireland.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: RS election is from South Africa and RS nomination is from Ireland, so both statements are correct.

s: From which country was the method of election of the President of India borrowed?
x: The President's election method and nomination to the Rajya Sabha came from Ireland; South Africa gave the amendment procedure and Rajya Sabha elections.

s: Which country has the world's first written Constitution, also the shortest with only 7 Articles?
x: The USA has the first and shortest written Constitution (7 Articles); Britain has no single written constitution.

s: Which one of the following is correct about Article 21?
o: It uses 'procedure established by law', borrowed from Japan
It was borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935
It uses 'procedure established by law', borrowed from Ireland
It uses 'due process of law', borrowed from the USA
x: Article 21 uses 'procedure established by law', an expression borrowed from Japan; it does not use 'due process of law'.

s: From which country was the post of Vice-President in the Indian Constitution borrowed?
x: The Vice-President's post came from the USA, along with impeachment and removal of judges.

s: From the Constitution of which country was the impeachment of the President borrowed?
x: Impeachment of the President is a US feature.

s: Judicial review in India is narrower than in the USA because Article 21 uses which phrase?
x: Article 21 uses 'procedure established by law' (from Japan), not the US 'due process'.

s: From which country was the procedure for removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges borrowed?
x: The removal of SC and HC judges, like the impeachment of the President, was borrowed from the USA.

s: Which Articles of the Constitution contain the Fundamental Rights borrowed from the USA?
x: Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12 to 35, on the US model.

s: From which country was the idea of the Preamble in the Indian Constitution borrowed?
x: The idea of the Preamble came from the USA; France gave liberty, equality, fraternity and the Republic.

s: From which country was the independence of the judiciary borrowed?
x: Independence of the judiciary, like judicial review, came from the USA.

s: From which country did India borrow the parliamentary system and its conventions?
x: The parliamentary system and its conventions came from Britain, even though Britain has no single written Constitution.

s: From which country was single citizenship in the Indian Constitution borrowed?
x: Single citizenship, like bicameralism and the cabinet system, came from Britain; the USA has dual citizenship.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Parliamentary privileges — United States of America
x: Prerogative writs were borrowed from Britain. Parliamentary privileges, bicameralism and the office of Speaker were also associated with the British constitutional model, not the countries stated in the other options.

s: From which country was bicameralism in the Indian Constitution borrowed?
x: Bicameralism, like the cabinet system and single citizenship, came from Britain (APPSC GS 2024).

s: From which country was the office of the Speaker and his role borrowed?
x: The office of Speaker is a British parliamentary feature.

s: Which of the following was NOT borrowed from Britain?
x: Judicial review came from the USA; single citizenship, Rule of Law and the cabinet system came from Britain.

s: From which country were parliamentary privileges in the Indian Constitution borrowed?
x: Parliamentary privileges, like the Speaker's office and prerogative writs, came from Britain.

s: What is a system in which a single hierarchy of courts enforces both Central and State laws called?
x: India has an integrated judiciary with one hierarchy of courts for both Central and State laws, unlike the separate federal and State courts of the USA.

s: From the Constitution of which country was the vesting of residuary powers in the Centre borrowed?
x: Residuary powers with the Centre came from Canada; Australia gave the joint sitting and freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse.

s: Who presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament under Article 108?
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
x: A joint sitting under Article 108, itself an Australian borrowing, is presided over by the Speaker.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with its source?
o: Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse — Canada
Nominal head comparable to the Crown — Britain
x: Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse was borrowed from Australia, not Canada. The other three pairs are correctly matched.

s: From which country was the idea of a federation with a strong Centre borrowed?
x: A federation with a strong Centre came from Canada; the Concurrent List came from Australia.

s: From which country was the provision for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament borrowed?
x: The joint sitting, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse, and the language of the Preamble came from Australia.

s: Under which Article do residuary powers lie with Parliament in India?
x: Article 248 vests residuary powers in Parliament, following Canada; in the USA and Australia they lie with the States.

s: From which country was the appointment of State Governors by the Centre borrowed?
x: Appointment of Governors by the Centre came from Canada.

s: What happens if a Union law and a State law clash on a Concurrent List subject?
x: Both Parliament and State Legislatures legislate on the Concurrent List, but the Union law prevails in a clash.

s:
Consider the following statements about federal features borrowed by the Constitution:
1. Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse was borrowed from Australia.
2. The Concurrent List was borrowed from Canada.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and the Concurrent List both came from Australia, not Canada.

s: From which country was the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Article 143) borrowed?
x: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143 was taken from Canada.

s: Which Article of the Constitution describes India as a 'Union of States'?
x: Article 1 calls India a 'Union of States', on the Canadian pattern: not the result of an agreement, and no State can secede.

s:
Consider the following statements about India as a 'Union of States':
1. It is the result of an agreement among the States.
2. No State has the right to secede from it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among States, and States have no right to secede.

s: How many subjects does the Union List of the Seventh Schedule now contain?
x: The Union, State and Concurrent Lists now contain 98, 59 and 52 subjects respectively.

s: Originally, the State List of the Seventh Schedule contained how many subjects?
x: The lists were originally 97, 66 and 47; now they are 98, 59 and 52.

s: Under which Article is the joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament provided?
x: Article 108 provides for the joint sitting, borrowed from Australia; Article 143 is advisory jurisdiction.

s: How many subjects does the Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule now contain?
x: The Concurrent List now has 52 subjects (originally 47); the Union List 98 and the State List 59.

s: From the Constitution of which country was the language of the Preamble borrowed?
x: The language of the Preamble came from Australia, while the GoI Act, 1935 gave the Constitution its structural and administrative backbone.

s: The Indian Constitution is criticised as a 'bag of borrowings' mainly because it:
o: Drew many provisions from foreign constitutions
x: The criticism refers to the large number of provisions drawn from foreign constitutions and earlier laws; length is the 'elephantine' criticism and legal detail the 'lawyers' paradise' one.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the borrowed parts of the Indian Constitution?
o: The parliamentary system forms part of the political part.
The structure is largely drawn from the Government of India Act, 1935.
Directive Principles form part of the political part.
Fundamental Rights form part of the philosophical part.
x: Directive Principles, like Fundamental Rights, belong to the philosophical part; the parliamentary system is the political part.

s: How many Articles, Parts and Schedules did the original Constitution of India contain?
x: The original Constitution had 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; today it has about 470 Articles, 25 Parts and 12 Schedules.

s: To which of the following did critics who called the Indian Constitution a 'lawyers' paradise' point?
x: 'Lawyers' paradise' refers to its legal detail; 'elephantine' refers to its length and 'bag of borrowings' to its sources.

s: Why is the Indian Constitution called the lengthiest written constitution in the world?
o: It was drawn from many sources and the GoI Act 1935, with much detail
It was written in many languages
x: Drawing on most of the world's constitutions and the detailed 1935 Act made it the lengthiest written constitution.

s: To what did critics point when they called the Indian Constitution 'elephantine'?
x: 'Elephantine' refers to its great length; 'lawyers' paradise' refers to its legal detail.

s: The three Lists under the Government of India Act, 1935 became which of the following in the Constitution of India?
o: Union List, Residuary List and Concurrent List
Central List, Provincial List and Local List
Union List, State List and Concurrent List
Federal List, Provincial List and State List
x: The Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists of the 1935 Act developed into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Constitution.

s: Which of the following is regarded as the single largest source of the provisions of the Indian Constitution?
o: The Constitution of the United States of America
x: The Government of India Act, 1935 is regarded as the single largest source, particularly for the federal scheme, Governor's office, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details.

s: The influence of the Government of India Act, 1935 is a major reason for which feature of the Indian Constitution?
o: Its bulk and extensive administrative detail
x: The 1935 Act contributed extensive administrative provisions, making the Indian Constitution unusually detailed and bulky.

s: By which of the following was the demand for a written Constitution made by Indians accepted in principle?
x: The 1935 Act did not provide for a Constitution made by Indians; the August Offer of 1940 accepted it in principle.

s: Which of the following features was NOT taken from the Government of India Act, 1935?
x: Fundamental Duties came from the USSR; the Governor, PSCs and Emergency scheme came from the 1935 Act.

s: With which of the following is suspension of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency associated?
x: Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency is associated with Weimar Germany; the general emergency scheme is associated with the 1935 Act.

s: Which Amendment Act added the eleventh Fundamental Duty?
x: Fundamental Duties were introduced by the 42nd Amendment (1976); the eleventh duty was added by the 86th Amendment.

s: Which Article is the most easily suspended during a National Emergency?
x: Article 19 is the most easily suspended; Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

s: From which country were the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble borrowed?
x: France gave the Republic and liberty, equality and fraternity; the USSR gave the ideals of justice.

s: From which country was the idea of Five-Year Plans borrowed?
x: Five-Year Plans and the Planning Commission idea came from the USSR.

s: Which Articles of the Constitution cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency?
x: During a National Emergency, Fundamental Rights can be suspended except Articles 20 and 21.

s: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution was borrowed from the USSR?
x: Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A) came from the USSR; DPSP is from Ireland, Republic from France and the Concurrent List from Australia.

s: Which of the following provisions of the Indian Constitution was NOT borrowed from any foreign constitution?
x: The Election Commission under Article 324 is an Indian provision not inspired by any foreign constitution; the others were borrowed.

s: From which country were the ideals of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble borrowed?
x: These ideals came from the USSR, not Australia; Australia gave the Concurrent List and freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse.

s: From which country was the ideal of a Republic in the Indian Constitution borrowed?
x: The ideal of a Republic, like liberty, equality and fraternity, was borrowed from France.

s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of features borrowed from the Constitution of the United States of America?
